# Parvovirus B19 infections

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric dermatology > Parvovirus B19 infections*

[Original Article Link](/library/G40BkT)

---

## Summary

<u>Parvovirus B19</u> is transmitted through respiratory droplets and has a wide range of clinical presentations. Infections occur most frequently in children, with peak <u>incidence</u> between 5 and 15 years of age (infection provides lifelong <u>immunity</u>). While most infections are asymptomatic, <u>erythema infectiosum</u> (<u>fifth disease</u>) is the most common clinical manifestation in symptomatic children. <u>Erythema infectiosum</u> begins with a mild <u>febrile</u> illness followed 7–10 days later by a <u>rash</u> with <u>macules</u> and <u>papules</u> that is especially noticeable on the cheeks (slapped‑cheek <u>rash</u>) and trunk and spreads to the extremities. The <u>rash</u> may be pruritic. Once the <u>rash</u> has appeared, the infection is no longer contagious and the patient usually feels well again, although the <u>rash</u> may persist for weeks, especially with heat and exposure to sunlight. In adults, the <u>rash</u> is typically absent and patients may develop acute-onset <u>polyarthralgia</u> (<u>parvovirus B19-associated arthritis</u>). Individuals who are <u>immunocompromised</u> and/or have preexisting hematological disease may develop <u>severe anemia</u> or <u>pancytopenia</u> because the <u>virus</u> affects the <u>bone marrow</u>. Diagnosis of <u>erythema infectiosum</u> is usually clinical; confirmatory studies are recommended for atypical presentations, pregnant patients (because of the risk of <u>congenital TORCH infection</u>), and <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>. Management is supportive.

## Etiology

### <u>Pathogen</u>




* Human <u>parvovirus B19</u> (the smallest of the <u>DNA viruses</u>)

* Family: <u>Parvoviridae</u>

* Single‑stranded <u>DNA virus</u> (linear)

* Nonenveloped

* Humans are the only reservoir for <u>parvovirus B19</u>.





### Route of transmission




* Main route: aerosol

* Other routes

* Hematogenous transmission

* Transplacental transmission: In seronegative pregnant women, transmission to the unborn fetus may occur (in up to 30% of cases).





### <u>Incubation period</u> [[2]](/library/Bedza60)




* Average: 4–14 days

* May be up to 21 days





References:[[3]](/library/rdafrj)[[4]](/library/rUafeP)

---

## Pathophysiology

* <u>Parvovirus B19</u> binds to the P antigen (<u>globoside</u>) on erythroid progenitor cells  → cellular invasion → viral <u>DNA</u> enters the <u>nucleus</u> of erythroid cells → viral <u>DNA</u> replication → cytotoxicity → clinical manifestations + transient cessation of <u>erythropoiesis</u> [[5]](/library/qQYCCK)[[6]](/library/IQYYxK)

* <u>Parvovirus B19</u> can also bind to and infect <u>endothelial</u> cells via the <u>P antigen</u>, potentially causing cardiovascular complications. [[7]](/library/ZlbZvF)[[8]](/library/YlbnvF)

---

## Clinical features

Individuals with <u>parvovirus B19</u> infection may be asymptomatic or have any of the following presentations (see “Subtypes and variants” for additional details). [[2]](/library/Bedza60)[[9]](/library/1Jd2GI0)




* Mild respiratory symptoms

* <u>Rash</u>

* <u>Erythema infectiosum</u> (<u>fifth disease</u>)

* <u>Papular</u>-<u>purpuric</u> gloves-and-socks syndrome

* Painful, pruritic, <u>papular</u>, <u>petechial</u>, and/or <u>purpuric</u> <u>rash</u> affecting the hands and feet

* <u>Fever</u> and oral lesions may be present.

* <u>Parvovirus B19-associated arthritis</u>

* <u>Severe anemia</u> or <u>transient aplastic crisis</u>

* <u>Hydrops fetalis</u>

* <u>Parvovirus B19</u> is a <u>TORCH infection</u> that can cause fetal <u>death</u> and <u>miscarriage</u>.

* See also “<u>Congenital parvovirus B19 infection</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Children with <u>parvovirus B19</u> infection often present with an <u>exanthem</u>, while adults are more likely to present with <u>arthritis</u>. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)[[10]](/library/XVY9GL)

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[11]](/library/GGdB070)[[12]](/library/GdaBrj)




* <u>Erythema infectiosum</u> and <u>parvovirus B19-associated arthritis</u> are <u>diagnosed clinically</u>.

* <u>Confirmatory studies for parvovirus B19</u> are recommended in:

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* <u>Immunocompromised individuals</u>

* Additional testing may be indicated for:

* Suspected <u>anemia</u> or <u>aplastic crisis</u> (e.g., in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>)

* Exclusion of alternative diagnoses (e.g., rheumatologic disease in patients with <u>arthritis</u>)

* See “Subtypes and variants” for details.





> [!WARNING]
> Congenital infection with <u>parvovirus B19</u> can cause severe complications; for more information on diagnosis during <u>pregnancy</u>, see “<u>Parvovirus B19 infection during pregnancy</u>.”




### Confirmatory studies for parvovirus B19




* Immunocompetent individuals: <u>IgM</u> and <u>IgG antibodies</u> [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* <u>IgM</u>: usually detectable when the <u>rash</u> appears; remains positive for 2–3 months

* <u>IgG</u>: positive after approx. 2 days; remains positive for life

* <u>Immunocompromised individuals</u>: <u>NAAT</u>  [[2]](/library/Bedza60)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Immunocompromised</u> patients may have <u>falsely negative</u> serum <u>IgM</u> and <u>IgG</u>. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

---

## Subtypes and variants

### Erythema infectiosum (<u>fifth disease</u>) [[2]](/library/Bedza60)




* Clinical features

* <u>Prodromal</u> stage: systemic symptoms occurring 7–10 days before <u>rash</u> [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* <u>Fever</u> (often mild)

* <u>Myalgia</u> and/or <u>arthralgias</u>

* <u>Malaise</u>

* <u>Headache</u>

* <u>Exanthem</u> stage: characteristic <u>rash</u>

* Slapped-cheek appearance; diffuse redness of the face with perioral sparing

* Reticular <u>rash</u> originating on the trunk and spreading to the extremities; adopts a lace‑like, reticular appearance over time as it clears.

* Often pruritic

* May recur with environmental changes (e.g., sunlight, heat exposure) over several weeks or months

* Diagnosis: <u>clinical diagnosis</u>

* Differential diagnoses

* Other <u>infectious rashes in childhood</u>

* <u>Drug hypersensitivity reaction</u>

* Management

* Management is supportive.

* See “<u>Management of parvovirus B19 infection</u>” for details.

### Parvovirus B19-associated arthritis [[2]](/library/Bedza60)[[10]](/library/XVY9GL)




* Clinical features

* Adults [[10]](/library/XVY9GL)

* Acute-onset <u>arthralgia</u> with symmetrical, nondestructive <u>polyarthritis</u>, particularly in <u>small joints</u> (fingers, hands), ankles, and knees

* Affects <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* <u>Rash</u>: absent or atypical

* May be accompanied by systemic symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>malaise</u>)

* Usually resolves within 2 weeks; may last months or years [[10]](/library/XVY9GL)

* Children (uncommon): most commonly affects the knees

* Diagnosis

* <u>Clinical diagnosis</u>

* In patients with diagnostic uncertainty:

* Obtain <u>confirmatory studies for parvovirus B19</u>.

* Consider additional studies to exclude alternative diagnoses (e.g., <u>diagnostics for rheumatoid arthritis</u>).

* Differential diagnoses

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* <u>Differential diagnoses of infection-associated arthritis</u>

* Management

* <u>NSAIDs</u> for <u>pain management</u>

* See “<u>Management of parvovirus B19 infection</u>” for details.





### <u>Parvovirus B19</u>-associated <u>anemia</u> [[2]](/library/Bedza60)




* Clinical features

* Symptoms of <u>pancytopenia</u> (e.g., <u>symptoms of anemia</u>, <u>symptoms of thrombocytopenia</u>)

* May be preceded by <u>fever</u>, <u>malaise</u>, and <u>myalgia</u>

* Chronic <u>pure red cell aplasia</u> occurs in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>.

* <u>Transient aplastic crisis</u> occurs in patients with chronic <u>hemolytic</u> diseases (e.g., <u>sickle cell disease</u>)

* Diagnosis

* Perform <u>confirmatory studies for parvovirus B19</u> in all patients.  [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* <u>CBC</u> and <u>reticulocyte count</u> [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* ↓ <u>Reticulocytes</u>

* ↓↓ <u>Hemoglobin</u>

* <u>Thrombocytopenia</u> and <u>leukopenia</u> in <u>transient aplastic crisis</u>

* Management

* Refer patients with <u>severe anemia</u> or <u>transient aplastic crisis</u> to <u>hematology</u>.

* <u>Blood transfusion</u> and IVIG may be required.

* See also “<u>Management of parvovirus B19 infection</u>.”

---

## Management

* Offer symptomatic treatment. [[13]](/library/rXdfzo0)

* <u>Arthralgia</u>: <u>NSAIDs</u> (for dosages, see “<u>Oral analgesics</u>” for adults and “<u>Nonopioid oral analgesia in children</u>”)

* <u>Pruritus</u>: Consider <u>antihistamines</u>.

* <u>Fever</u> (e.g., <u>antipyretics</u>, <u>supportive care for pediatric fever</u>)

* Provide specialist referral as indicated, e.g.:

* Obstetrics: all pregnant patients (and pregnant contacts); see also “<u>Congenital parvovirus B19 infection</u>.”

* <u>Hematology</u>: patients with <u>severe anemia</u> and <u>aplastic crisis</u>

* Educate on appropriate <u>infection control</u> measures. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Advise <u>hand hygiene</u> and <u>respiratory hygiene</u> for all patients and caregivers.

* Use <u>droplet precautions</u> for hospitalized patients with : [[2]](/library/Bedza60)[[14]](/library/CZ1qd20) 

* <u>Aplastic crisis</u>  [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* PPGSS

* <u>Immunosuppression</u> and <u>pure red cell aplasia</u>





> [!TIP]
> Children with the <u>rash</u> of <u>erythema infectiosum</u> are not contagious and do not require exclusion from school or daycare. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)
